title: Acute psychiatric ward: feasibility of nurse-delivered alcohol brief intervention, unverified landmark lead, cited record mismatched after acceptance
notes: Adversarial path on a clear feasibility question (routing explicit feasibility from 'We want to do a feasibility study'). A fixture search returns seven records with abstracts. The first scan reply (shape discovery) appends three leads after the records (D1): one is a model-labelled 'landmark' multicentre trial with the invented DOI 10.5555/ipj.2020.0412, high scores and no limitations, which must stay a model lead (origin model, status unverified, no checks; G3), and the reply's certainty 'high', justified by that lead, is refused (dropped, 'not assessed', no 'high certainty' label; G1, D20 with S13), while a lead with year null keeps year and methodQuality null (G4). The second scan reply (shape appraisal) annotates the seven records and records claims c1 to c4 with passages that are exact substrings of the abstracts; certainty 'low'. The design decision rests on c1 to c3 with the ethics gate unknown, so acceptance gives selection accepted and action blocked. Then, on the Design route, an identity check sets the status of the single-ward delivery study (cited by c1) to 'mismatch' through the store: the decision must become stale and blocked in the store, on screen and after reload, stay stale after reopen ('review required') and in the export, and Map to Design are flagged for review (G7, G8). Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts, computed by the generator script: DOI hash for records 2, 3, 5, 6 (ev-1g1zi9r, ev-0b805zr, ev-17n3313, ev-0ak0pfu); titleYearKey hash for records 1, 4, 7 (ev-1ab3aht, ev-08e12wz, ev-0c4i6wb). Requires D1 (leads appended), D20 and S13 (no certainty from a discovery reply; appraisal on the production path), S10 and S11 (stale invalidation, selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text). Catches: a model label or a DOI treated as verification, certainty raised by an unretrieved lead, and an accepted decision that stays current after its cited record is found to be a different work.

inputs.need:
I am a consultant psychiatrist on a 24-bed acute adult inpatient unit. About a third of the people we admit drink at harmful levels, and alcohol problems are recorded in the admission notes but rarely acted on: there is no routine screening on the ward, and referral to the community alcohol team happens for perhaps one patient in ten. Many of our nurses have been trained to deliver a brief motivational intervention in the general hospital, and we want to know whether a structured version could work on a psychiatric ward, where people are acutely unwell, sometimes detained, and often discharged within two weeks.

We want to do a feasibility study before anyone talks about a larger evaluation. The questions are practical: can nurses screen every admission with a short alcohol questionnaire once the person is well enough, how many screen positive, how many agree to a brief intervention of two sessions before discharge, whether the sessions are delivered as intended when the ward is busy, and whether we can reach people by phone three months after discharge to ask about their drinking. We would also like to hear from patients and nurses about whether the intervention is acceptable, and to check that it does not upset people who are already distressed.

The ward manager supports it, and the hospital research office has agreed to review a protocol. We have no research nurse, so screening and sessions would be part of the named nurse's normal work. I need help with progression criteria, the right follow-up measure, and how to stay honest about what a feasibility study can and cannot show.
inputs.constraints: No research nurse: screening and sessions must fit the named nurse's normal shifts. Patients who lack capacity to consent are not approached until capacity returns. Follow-up after discharge is by phone only. Recruitment must finish within nine months.
localFacts: The ward admitted 412 adults in the last 12 months; the admission notes recorded harmful drinking for 131 of them.
Eleven of the ward's 19 registered nurses completed the hospital's brief motivational intervention training in 2025.
The ward manager approved screening and two intervention sessions within the named nurse's shifts from January to September 2027 (approval WM-4A-2026-11).
The hospital research office agreed on 2026-09-10 to review a feasibility protocol; no research ethics committee opinion has been given yet.

records.title: Alcohol screening at admission to acute psychiatric wards: how many screen positive and how many are offered help
records.abstract: We reviewed 1,036 consecutive admissions to four acute adult psychiatric wards over one year. A three-item alcohol consumption questionnaire was completed for 61 percent of admissions, usually within three days, and 34 percent of those screened were positive for hazardous or harmful drinking. Only 22 percent of screen-positive patients had any documented alcohol intervention before discharge, and 9 percent were referred to specialist alcohol services. Screening was least often completed for patients admitted under detention and for those discharged within five days. Routine screening identifies many patients with alcohol problems, but in these wards identification rarely led to help.

records.title: Nurse-delivered brief motivational intervention for harmful drinking among psychiatric inpatients: a single-ward before-after feasibility study
records.authors: Quinlan-Adeyemi R, Marsh-Takahashi E, Oduya-Pellegrini S
records.abstract: We tested whether ward nurses could deliver a two-session brief motivational intervention to inpatients who screened positive for harmful drinking on one acute psychiatric ward. Over eight months, 52 patients screened positive and 41 agreed to take part. Nurses delivered both sessions before discharge to 38 of 52 patients who screened positive, and session recordings showed that 81 percent of core intervention components were delivered. Sessions were most often missed when patients were discharged at short notice. At three months, 24 of 41 participants were reached by telephone. No adverse events related to the intervention were recorded. Delivery by ward nurses appears possible; follow-up was the main difficulty.

records.title: Brief alcohol interventions for people with severe mental illness: a systematic review of trials
records.authors: Petrov-Mensah A, Gallagher-Osei L, Ibrahim-Sandoval K, Whitlock-Obi D
records.abstract: We searched five databases for trials of brief alcohol interventions in adults with severe mental illness. Fourteen trials met the inclusion criteria; only two recruited psychiatric inpatients, and both were small. Across trials, effects on drinking at six to twelve months were small and inconsistent, and most trials relied on self-reported drinking with high loss to follow-up. No trial reported harm from the intervention. Trials rarely described who delivered the intervention or how fidelity was checked. The evidence does not show whether brief interventions reduce drinking in this population, and inpatient delivery remains largely untested.

records.title: Reaching people by telephone three months after psychiatric discharge: response rates and data quality
records.abstract: We attempted structured telephone follow-up at three months for 214 adults discharged from two acute psychiatric wards who had agreed to be contacted. Telephone follow-up at three months after psychiatric discharge reached 46 percent of participants, after up to five call attempts. People who were homeless at discharge or had changed their phone number were least often reached. Among those reached, self-reported alcohol use agreed moderately with information in community records. Offering a text message before the call and collecting a second contact number at discharge increased the response rate in the last four months of the study.

records.title: Acceptability of discussing alcohol during acute psychiatric admission: accounts from patients and nurses
records.abstract: We held semi-structured conversations with 18 inpatients and 12 nurses on two acute psychiatric wards about discussing alcohol during admission. Patients described being asked about alcohol during admission as acceptable when the question came from their named nurse after the acute crisis had settled. Several patients said that questions asked on the day of admission felt like an accusation. Nurses worried about damaging the therapeutic relationship and about having no time to follow up what patients disclosed. Both groups preferred a short conversation linked to a plan for after discharge. Participants were recruited by ward staff, which may have favoured positive accounts.

records.title: Progression criteria in feasibility studies of ward-based interventions: a methodological review
records.authors: Nakamura-Holt S, Osei-Brandt W, Vasquez-Lind R
records.abstract: We reviewed 58 published feasibility studies of interventions delivered on hospital wards to see whether they stated criteria for progressing to a larger evaluation. Only 21 of 58 feasibility studies stated progression criteria in advance, and 9 of those used a traffic-light system with green, amber and red thresholds. Studies without pre-stated criteria were more likely to describe their findings as promising whatever their recruitment and retention. Few studies reported confidence intervals for feasibility estimates. We recommend stating progression criteria before recruitment, with thresholds for recruitment, delivery and follow-up, and reporting feasibility estimates with their precision.

records.title: Fidelity of nurse-delivered brief interventions during busy shifts: an observational study on medical and psychiatric wards
records.abstract: We observed 96 brief intervention sessions delivered by nurses on medical and psychiatric wards and rated fidelity against a checklist of core components. Mean fidelity was 72 percent on medical wards and 64 percent on psychiatric wards. Fidelity fell when the nurse was also responsible for more than six patients and when the session was interrupted. Sessions delivered in a quiet room scored higher than bedside sessions. Nurses said a pocket card with the core steps helped them keep sessions short and complete. The observer was present in every session, which may have raised fidelity.

steps.note: Seven records with abstracts; ids are stableRecordId values computed by the generator (see notes).

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Screening on psychiatric wards finds many patients with harmful drinking but rarely leads to help. One single-ward study shows nurses can deliver a two-session intervention to most screen-positive patients, while three-month telephone follow-up reaches only about half of patients. Patients accept alcohol questions from their named nurse once the crisis has settled. Trials in severe mental illness show small, inconsistent effects and rarely include inpatients, so effectiveness is not the question for this study. Feasibility studies often lack pre-stated progression criteria. The three leads suggested by the discovery reply were not retrieved and are not appraised.

response.reading: The pathway runs from admission, through a period when the patient becomes well enough to talk, to a short window for two sessions before an often abrupt discharge, and then to a follow-up call that about half of patients answer. Each step can fail for reasons unrelated to the intervention's value: detention, short stays, ward workload and lost phone numbers. The retrieved evidence gives planning values for delivery (c1), follow-up (c2) and acceptability (c3); the lead presented as a landmark trial is unverified and plays no part.

store.title: Feasibility of nurse-delivered alcohol screening and brief intervention on an acute psychiatric ward

response.overview: Single-ward feasibility study, January to September 2027: named nurses screen eligible admissions with a short alcohol questionnaire once the patient is well enough, offer screen-positive patients a two-session brief motivational intervention before discharge, and attempt telephone follow-up three months after discharge. Progression criteria are stated before recruitment. The planning value for delivery came from a record whose identity check failed after the design was accepted; it is kept only as a flagged value until re-appraised.
response.population: Adults admitted to the 24-bed acute unit, screened once the named nurse judges them well enough and able to consent; people lacking capacity are approached only when capacity returns; stays shorter than 48 hours are excluded.
response.exposure: Two sessions of 20 to 30 minutes by a trained named nurse, using a pocket card of core steps, with a written plan for after discharge and an offer of referral to the community alcohol team.
response.procedures: Screening within the first well-enough day; consent by the named nurse; sessions in a quiet room where possible; a fidelity checklist completed after each session, with 20 percent of sessions audio-recorded and rated by a second trained nurse; two contact numbers and consent for a text reminder collected before discharge; three-month call by a nurse from another ward, up to five attempts.

outcomes.name: Uptake of the intervention
outcomes.measure: Proportion of screen-positive patients who consent and receive at least the first session before discharge
outcomes.why: The central feasibility question and the basis of any future sample size.

outcomes.name: Screening completion
outcomes.measure: Proportion of eligible admissions screened before discharge, by detention status and length of stay
outcomes.why: Shows whether the patients most at risk are reached.

outcomes.name: Delivery and fidelity
outcomes.measure: Proportion receiving both sessions; percentage of core components delivered on the checklist
outcomes.why: Separates a failed idea from failed delivery.

outcomes.name: Three-month follow-up completion
outcomes.measure: Proportion of participants reached by phone with a completed drinking question
outcomes.why: Retention is the step most likely to block a larger study.

outcomes.name: Distress after sessions
outcomes.measure: Patient-rated distress (0 to 10) before and after each session; any incident linked to a session
outcomes.why: The intervention must not add distress on an acute ward.

response.feasibility: About 250 eligible admissions over nine months; eleven trained nurses; sessions within approved shift time (WM-4A-2026-11); follow-up calls by nurses from another ward within normal duties.

response.designSummary: Descriptive feasibility estimates with 95 percent confidence intervals, judged against pre-stated traffic-light progression criteria.
response.sampleSize: The ward admits about 309 adults in nine months; if about 80 percent are screenable before discharge and about a third screen positive (the local notes record harmful drinking in 131 of 412 admissions), about 80 patients will screen positive. An uptake of 50 percent among 80 patients is estimated with a 95 percent confidence interval of about plus or minus 11 percentage points, enough to tell a green threshold (40 percent or more) from a red one (below 25 percent). No formal power calculation applies because no comparison is made.
response.primaryAnalysis: Uptake proportion with a Wilson 95 percent confidence interval, compared with the progression thresholds: green 40 percent or more, amber 25 to 39 percent, red below 25 percent.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Screening completion by detention status and length of stay; proportion receiving both sessions; mean fidelity with its interval; three-month follow-up completion (green 60 percent or more); change in session distress ratings, descriptive.
response.missingData: Missing screening, session or follow-up data are counted as not done for the feasibility proportions; reasons are recorded and reported.
response.multiplicity: No hypothesis tests; each estimate is reported with its interval against its own pre-stated threshold.
response.software: R for proportions and intervals; the progression thresholds are archived before recruitment.
overfittingGuards: Thresholds fixed before the first patient is screened
No subgroup comparisons beyond the two pre-stated breakdowns
Drinking outcomes at three months described only, never tested
response.summary: About 80 screen-positive patients give an uptake estimate within about 11 percentage points; traffic-light criteria decide progression.

response.risks: Low: two conversations with a trained nurse and a follow-up call. Risks are distress when discussing alcohol during an acute episode, pressure to take part felt by detained patients, and disclosure of risk during follow-up calls.
response.consent: Written informed consent by the named nurse only when the patient is judged to have capacity; detained patients are told that declining has no effect on their care or detention; consent for follow-up calls and text reminders is separate.
response.data: Screening results and session checklists are held in a study file on the hospital network with a study number; audio recordings are deleted after fidelity rating; follow-up answers are entered directly into the study file.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: detained patients, people who are homeless at discharge, people without a phone and people with limited English are the least likely to be screened, to take part and to be reached. Screening and uptake are reported by detention status and length of stay, interpreters are used for sessions, and a second contact route is agreed before discharge.
response.effectiveness: The study succeeds if it decides whether a larger evaluation is feasible; it will not claim any effect on drinking.
response.efficiency: Uses approved nurse time and existing training; no new staff.
response.costs: Printing, a recording device and nurse time within normal shifts; follow-up calls within normal duties of another ward.
response.grants: None needed; a positive result would support an application for a comparative evaluation.
response.partnerships: Community alcohol team (referral and advice), two people with lived experience of admission and drinking (materials and follow-up wording), and the ward's nursing team.
response.rebPath: Research ethics committee review of the feasibility protocol through the hospital research office, following ICH-GCP and the Declaration of Helsinki; the opinion is not yet given, so no patient is approached before it.
response.limitations: One ward; nurses know they are being observed; follow-up by phone may miss the patients doing worst.
response.summary: Low-risk study with capacity safeguards, equity reporting by detention status and an ethics opinion still awaited.

response.title: Nurse-delivered alcohol screening and brief intervention on an acute psychiatric ward: a feasibility study
response.abstract: Objectives: to estimate screening, uptake, delivery, fidelity and three-month follow-up for nurse-delivered alcohol screening and a two-session brief intervention on an acute psychiatric ward, against pre-stated progression criteria. Design: single-ward feasibility study, January to September 2027. Results and conclusions will be written after follow-up.
response.introduction: Harmful drinking is common among psychiatric inpatients but rarely addressed during admission. Retrieved studies suggest nurses can deliver brief interventions and patients accept them once the crisis settles, while follow-up after discharge is difficult; trials in this population are few and mostly outpatient.
response.methods: Named nurses screen eligible admissions once the patient is well enough, offer two sessions before discharge, and complete fidelity checklists; nurses from another ward make three-month follow-up calls. Traffic-light progression criteria were stated before recruitment.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the screening-to-follow-up flow, each proportion with its interval and traffic-light rating, fidelity, and session distress ratings.
response.discussion: The discussion will judge progression against the pre-stated criteria, describe who was missed, and state what the study cannot show about effectiveness. The planning value for delivery will be discussed only after its source is re-appraised.
response.limitations: One ward; observed delivery; phone-only follow-up; one planning value rests on a record whose identity check failed.
response.conclusion: To be written after follow-up; it will address feasibility and progression only.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for pilot and feasibility studies (non-comparative items) with TIDieR
response.summary: Feasibility report draft with results left empty.
